subtitle: Words that join sentences, and building an argument
words.intro: In 2020 the whole country went home to work. Germans discovered that a meeting can go ahead with a cat in it. Some people never went back, and some bosses still can’t believe it.

grammar[0].fact: German has three ways of joining with one meaning: *weil es regnet* (verb last), *denn es regnet* (verb stays), *es regnet, deshalb* (verb next). Learners tend to think these are the same. They are, until you write them down.

grammar[1].blocks[0].title: The shape of a paragraph
grammar[1].blocks[0].note: Claim, reason, other side, turn, result. Five sentences, and it sounds like an argument.
grammar[1].blocks[1].title: Words that weigh
grammar[1].blocks[1].items[0].en: on the one hand … on the other
grammar[1].blocks[2].title: Pick one side at the end
grammar[1].blocks[2].text: A German essay may spend pages weighing things, but the last line must say what you think. *Einerseits … andererseits* with no conclusion is a classic mark-losing move.
grammar[1].fact: German essays are taught in a shape: *These, Antithese, Synthese*, thesis, antithesis, synthesis. Hegel is often blamed. Twelve-year-olds learn it, and you may hear it at breakfast from a teenager who doesn’t want to tidy up.

document.intro: Two pages of a real, old union pay deal for leather workers. It is why your working week looks as it does. You can follow it, because it’s numbered. Look up the hours.
document.fact: German unions and employers negotiate such deals for each sector. The 48-hour week became 40 hours only after long fights, with Saturday going first: *Samstags gehört Vati mir*, on Saturdays Daddy belongs to me, ran the famous union slogan of 1956.
document.tasks[1].instruction: Complete with zwar, aber, trotzdem or deshalb.
reading.title: Du bist stumm
reading.intro: A Monday in the online meeting. Eighteen faces, in eighteen small squares. Max’s company has had no office for three years, and he has never met his boss in person. Today the boss, Frau Ahrens, has something important to announce. She’s also on mute.
reading.photos[0].caption: Coworking: Außerdem gibt es hier Kaffee.
reading.fact: Germany has argued about a legal right to work from home since 2020, and has never quite passed one. Working-time rules still apply at home. So a German at the kitchen table is, officially, still at a workplace with rules on rest breaks.
